titre: The Well-Tempered Clavier Is Not What Its Name Suggests
accroche: “Well-tempered” does not mean what people generally think, and no one knows for certain what Bach really meant by it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1722, Johann Sebastian Bach completes in Köthen the first book of *The Well-Tempered Clavier*, twenty-four preludes and twenty-four fugues, one for each major and minor key. A second book will follow some twenty years later in Leipzig. The whole, forty-eight pieces in all, will become one of the most played and most studied works in the keyboard repertoire.

Today, the title of the work is often associated with “equal temperament,” the tuning system now universal, in which the octave is divided into twelve perfectly identical semitones. This association is intuitive, and for a good part of the 20th century, musicologists themselves assumed that Bach was aiming at equal temperament. It is, however, very probably wrong.

## What “well-tempered” really meant

The idea first appears in 1681 from the pen of the theorist Andreas Werckmeister: the subtitle of his treatise *Orgelprobe* promises to explain how to “temper well” (*wohl zu temperiren*) a keyboard. The two words will later fuse into the adjective *wohltemperiert*, the one Bach will take up for his own title in 1722. Neither Werckmeister's original phrase nor the adjective that grows out of it designates a single, precise system, but a family of temperaments designed so that one could play in all keys without running into an unusable interval, what was then called a “wolf interval,” too out of tune to be played in music.

These “well-tempered” temperaments reach that goal without making all semitones rigorously equal to one another: in most of these systems, each key keeps a slightly different harmonic color from the others, some intervals remaining purer than others. Equal temperament is, as the Encyclopaedia Britannica specifies, only one possible example of a “well-tempered” system among others, neither the only one available nor the one most commonly used in Bach's day.

Which precise temperament did Bach have in mind in writing his title? The question remains open: no document in his hand specifies it. The earliest testimonies are indirect: those of Forkel, Bach's first biographer, those of Marpurg, who gathers information from the composer's sons and students, and those of Kirnberger, one of those students. Marpurg and Kirnberger agree on at least one point: Bach wanted major thirds sharper than pure thirds. That is not enough to settle the matter, and musicologists continue to debate it, each proposing a reconstruction of the exact temperament Bach had in mind.

## What it shifts

The stakes are not only historical. A harpsichord tuned in equal temperament and another tuned in a period temperament do not sound the same: in the second case, each key keeps its own tint, softer or more tense depending on the intervals it uses, a relief that equal temperament, precisely because it makes everything uniform, erases. What Bach wanted listeners to hear in running through the twenty-four keys was perhaps not their likeness, but their differences.

repere.texte: In 1681, the German theorist Andreas Werckmeister promises, in the subtitle of his treatise Orgelprobe, to explain how to “temper well” (wohl zu temperiren) a keyboard; the two words only fuse into the adjective “wohltemperiert” afterward. In it he describes a family of temperaments allowing play in all keys, none of which imposes rigorously equal semitones.

carte.punch: “Well-tempered” doesn't mean what you think, and no one knows what Bach meant by it.
carte.idee: Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier (1722) is often associated with modern equal temperament. But well-tempered designated, as early as 1681, a whole family of systems in which each key keeps its own color. Which precise temperament Bach aimed at remains debated.

quiz.question: What did the expression “well-tempered” actually mean when Werckmeister first used it in 1681?
choix: A tuning in which the twelve semitones of the octave are made rigorously identical to one another
A family of temperaments allowing play in all keys without an unusable interval, without imposing equal semitones
A method reserved exclusively for the organ, inapplicable to the harpsichord or clavichord
A tuning strictly personal to Bach, which no other composer of his time used
quiz.explication: For Werckmeister, the term designated a family of temperaments allowing play in all keys without running into an unusable interval, while leaving each key a different harmonic color. Equal temperament, which makes the semitones rigorously identical, is only one example among others, popularized after the fact and often wrongly confused with the term itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the testimonies of Marpurg and Kirnberger reveal about Bach's intentions?
choix: That Bach wanted major thirds sharper than pure thirds
That Bach demanded a rigorous equal temperament for all his works
That Bach categorically refused to use Werckmeister's temperament
That Bach had never given any indication about the temperament of his works
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Marpurg, who gathers information from Bach's sons and students, and Kirnberger, one of those students, agree on at least one point: Bach wanted major thirds sharper than pure thirds. That is not enough to settle which precise temperament he aimed at.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What separates modern equal temperament from the 18th-century “well-tempered” temperaments?
choix: Equal temperament makes all semitones rigorously identical, erasing the color specific to each key
Equal temperament only allows play in one key at a time
The 18th-century well-tempered temperaments forbade playing in minor keys
Equal temperament was invented by Bach himself for his own works
quiz_supplementaire.explication: “Well-tempered” temperaments allowed play in all keys without an unusable interval, while leaving each a different harmonic color. Equal temperament, by making the semitones rigorously identical, makes everything uniform and erases that relief between keys.
